text.en: The Sun rises and sets each day. The Moon changes shape through the month. The year brings summer and winter. All come from how Earth, Moon and Sun move.

Earth spins on its axis once in 24 hours. This is rotation and it causes day and night. Earth also goes around the Sun once in about 365 and a quarter days. This is revolution. Earth's axis is tilted. Because of the tilt and the revolution we get seasons.
When the northern part of Earth is tilted towards the Sun it gets more direct light for longer and has summer. When it is tilted away it has winter.
The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. As it goes round Earth in about a month we see different parts of its lit side, called phases. From new moon, when it is not seen, the lit part grows to full moon and then shrinks again.
A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth and blocks the Sun's light. A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth comes between the Sun and Moon and its shadow falls on the Moon. Ask an adult to help you watch a projection or use safe solar viewing glasses. Ordinary sunglasses do not protect your eyes when looking at the Sun.

Imagine looking down on Earth’s North Pole. Earth spins eastward. This makes the Sun appear to move across our sky towards the west.

board.text: Earth rotates from west to east

text.en: At any one time the side facing the Sun gets daylight. Locations on the far side experience night.
On a globe, rotate a marked town towards the lit side. Sunrise occurs as that town moves into sunlight.
Keep the globe turning. Sunset occurs when the town rotates out of the lit side and into the night side.

board.text: Sunset: the place leaves the lit side

text.en: Earth’s rotation gives a day. Its trip around the Sun, called revolution, gives a year.

board.text: One day and one year describe different motions

text.en: At night we look into space away from the Sun’s general direction. Months later, Earth will be on a different part of its orbit.

board.text: The night side looks away from the Sun

text.en: As Earth moves, the night side faces different directions in space. Some familiar star patterns are easier to see in one part of the year than another.

board.text: Look for different stars in different months

text.en: When you carry a tilted globe around a lamp, keep its axis aimed in the same direction. The part tilted towards the lamp changes during the orbit.

board.text: Keep the tilt pointing in the same direction

text.en: Point a torch squarely at a surface, then angle it. The beam spreads over more area at a slant, giving each small patch less light.

board.text: More direct sunlight delivers more energy per area

text.en: When the north tilts towards the Sun, it gets longer days and stronger sunlight. The south gets shorter days and is in winter.
Across the orbit, the south tilts towards the Sun and the north tilts away. The pattern of seasons reverses.
Both hemispheres share almost the same Earth-to-Sun distance. Their opposite seasons follow from the tilt and the way sunlight falls.

board.text: Distance is not what makes opposite seasons

text.en: Sunlight usually illuminates half of the Moon. From Earth, the part of that lit half we can see changes as the Moon orbits.

board.text: Moon phases depend on our view

text.en: Near new Moon we see little of the lit half. At first quarter about half the visible disc looks lit. At full Moon almost the whole visible disc is lit.
Ordinary phases are changes in our view of the lit portion. A lunar eclipse instead occurs when Earth’s shadow actually reaches the Moon.

board.text: A phase is different from an eclipse

text.en: When the Moon passes directly in front of the Sun as seen from part of Earth, it casts a shadow on that region.
The Moon’s shadow covers a limited part of Earth. Viewers far from that path may see a partial eclipse or none at all.
Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon directly. People on much of Earth’s night side can see the lunar eclipse if the sky is clear.
Usually the Moon passes above or below the straight line between Earth and the Sun. A full or new Moon alone is not enough to produce an eclipse.
Face away from the Sun and watch its image fall onto a surface using a projector. The image shows the eclipse without your eyes facing the Sun.

board.text: Use an indirect view with adult guidance

text.en: The opening is for sunlight to pass through onto the viewing surface. To watch the eclipse, keep your eyes on the projected image.

board.text: Never look through the projector’s hole

text.en: Put the three objects in order and find which casts the shadow. A Moon shadow on Earth is solar. An Earth shadow on the Moon is lunar.
Earth rotates once in 24 hours.
The side facing the Sun has day; the other has night.

problem.en: Why can some constellations be easier to see at night in one month than another?

text.en: Mark Earth on two different parts of its orbit.

why.en: Its nightside faces away from the Sun in both positions.

text.en: The two nightsides face different directions in space.

why.en: The background constellations that can be seen at night change through the year.

problem.en: In a model, sunlight meets Earth first and the Moon is inside Earth’s shadow. Which eclipse is modelled?

text.en: Read the order: Sun, Earth, Moon.

why.en: Earth is between the light source and the Moon.

text.en: This is a lunar eclipse.

why.en: The Moon passes through Earth’s shadow.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking seasons come from distance to the Sun.

points.en: Eclipses occur when Sun, Moon and Earth line up.
